name: GHK-Cu
lead: GHK-Cu is the copper(II) complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (GHK), a short chain of three amino acids that binds copper strongly. It was first isolated from human plasma and is also found in saliva and urine [1]. In cosmetics it is listed as copper tripeptide-1 and appears in serums, creams, eye products and hair-care formulas sold for firming, smoothing and the look of fine lines [1][2][8].

People use it to look better in two broad ways. The first is topical: a copper peptide serum or cream applied to the face, sometimes combined with microneedling, aimed at skin thickness, firmness and fine lines. The second is the injectable research-peptide route, where GHK-Cu is sold in vials and often combined with other peptides in blends; users on looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums describe it as the skin and hair component of those stacks [17][20]. The chain proponents describe runs from more collagen and glycosaminoglycan in the dermis, to firmer, denser skin, to a younger-looking face.

Plasma GHK is reported to average about 200 ng/ml at age 20 and about 80 ng/ml by age 60, a decline that proponents often cite as the rationale for replacing it [1][3]. Laboratory and animal studies describe stimulation of collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, wound-healing effects, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity and changes in the expression of many genes [1][4]. In people, the published cosmetic work consists of small 4- to 12-week studies of GHK-Cu creams in women with photoaged skin, plus a randomized trial of copper tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing [11][12][27].

The US FDA lists injectable GHK-Cu among bulk drug substances nominated for compounding and later withdrawn, and states that compounded injectable drugs containing it may pose a risk of immunogenicity, with limited human data available [7]. Sports medicine reviews describe unapproved peptides sold for injection as part of a gray market operating largely outside regulatory oversight [5][6].

paras: GHK-Cu is widely used in anti-aging and hair-loss-prevention cosmetics [1]. A retail copper peptide facial serum listed on DailyMed is labelled to repair, tighten and address signs of premature aging, with external-use-only warnings [8]. Reviews discuss GHK as a topical anti-wrinkle peptide and describe it as a signal peptide that supports collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan synthesis and as a carrier peptide that delivers copper [2][27]. A palmitoylated derivative (Pal-GHK), the palmitoyl tripeptide-1 in Matrixyl 3000, was reported to be the second most used anti-wrinkle peptide in 2018 [27].

On looksmax.org, users ask whether GHK-Cu will help fine lines or an inflamed complexion, compare it with the peptide Matrixyl and with isotretinoin, and discuss pairing a topical with microneedling [28][29][30][31]. One reply in a microneedling thread states that topical plus microneedling beats a topical alone, and that a more invasive facial technique beats both [28].

GHK-Cu is not an approved drug. It is studied for wound healing and tissue repair. A registered phase 2 trial of topical GHK-Cu gel for acute skin wounds (punch biopsy wounds, 60 participants) began recruiting in 2026 [10]. A randomized trial examined copper tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing [11].

The story starts with Loren Pickart (1938 to 2023). Wikipedia traces the background to 1968 work by Pilgeram and Pickart on fibrinogen, and records that in 1973 Pickart isolated an activity from human plasma albumin after observing that liver tissue from older donors behaved more like young tissue when incubated in younger donors' blood; this was reported in Nature in May 1973 [1][13]. In 1977 the growth-modulating peptide was identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, and in 1980 Pickart and colleagues proposed that it helps move copper into cells [1][12].

A 2015 review lists later milestones: Downey and colleagues reported accelerated wound healing with GHK-Cu in 1985, Maquart and colleagues showed stimulated collagen synthesis in fibroblast cultures in 1988, Wegrowski and colleagues showed increased glycosaminoglycan synthesis in 1992, and Pickart received US patents on mixed copper-peptide compositions in 1995 and 1996 [12][32][33]. The authors of the 2015 and 2018 reviews are affiliated with a skin biology research company, and the 2018 authors state that their own gene analyses are computational and correlational [4][12].

sections.h: How it is thought to work

paras: GHK has a very high affinity for copper. Copper(II) is coordinated by the histidine imidazole nitrogen, the glycine amino nitrogen and a deprotonated amide nitrogen, and Wikipedia gives a stability constant far higher than that of the related glycyl-histidine complex [1]. The copper's redox activity is described as largely silenced when bound, which proponents say allows delivery into cells without free-copper oxidative damage [1][12].

The GHK sequence occurs within the alpha-2 chain of type I collagen and in SPARC, and it has been proposed that proteases release it after injury as an emergency repair signal that attracts repair cells and starts remodelling [1][12][13]. In cell work GHK-Cu stimulated collagen synthesis in skin fibroblasts at picomolar to nanomolar concentrations (1988), increased sulfated glycosaminoglycan synthesis (1992) and decorin synthesis, and stimulated both matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors (2000), so its reported effect is on tissue turnover as well as production [1][12][34][35].

Using the Broad Institute's Connectivity Map, Pickart and Margolina's 2018 narrative review reports that GHK changes the expression of about 31 percent of human genes by 50 percent or more, with 59 percent of those up-regulated, and the 2015 review cites at least 4,000 genes and increased expression of 47 DNA-repair genes [4][12]. The authors argue this suggests a wide, partly copper-independent mode of action and a 'resetting' of gene patterns toward a healthier state; they also state that links between gene signatures and outcomes are inferred rather than experimentally tested [4]. A 2012 review extends the discussion to oxidative stress and cognitive aging [16].

A 2025 review of topically applied GHK as an anti-wrinkle peptide describes the peptide's capacity for tissue regeneration and its promotion of collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, while discussing advantages, problems and prospects [2]. A 2018 review concludes that GHK has multiple actions that it characterizes as health positive in light of gene-expression data [4].

Most mechanistic findings come from cell cultures and animals, such as stimulation of collagen synthesis by fibroblasts and improved wound healing in rabbits, rats, mice and pigs [1][12][13]. Orthopaedic and sports medicine reviews list GHK-Cu among wound-healing peptides but frame the human evidence for injectable use as limited [5][6][14].

The 2015 review in BioMed Research International describes four human skin studies of GHK-Cu creams, none with statistics given in the review [12]. In a one-month thigh study (Abdulghani and colleagues, 1998), women around age 50 applied creams, and procollagen production rose in 70 percent of GHK-Cu users, versus 50 percent with a vitamin C cream and 40 percent with retinoic acid; the 2025 review describes it as a 20-volunteer split-body comparison [12][27]. Leyden and colleagues reported a 12-week facial study in 71 women with mild to advanced photoaging, with improved laxity, clarity and appearance, reduced fine lines and wrinkle depth, and increased skin density and thickness, and a 12-week eye-cream study in 41 women against placebo and a vitamin K cream with similar findings [12][27]. A 12-week twice-daily study by Finkley and colleagues in 67 women aged 50 to 59 reported improved firmness, fewer coarse wrinkles and less mottled pigmentation, with biopsies showing increased keratinocyte proliferation [12].

The 2025 BioImpacts review notes that clinical data for GHK-Cu are scarce, with the cited human studies small or available only as conference abstracts, and states that no safety studies on these peptides have been published [27]. Wikipedia likewise describes the controlled facial studies as small and short and flags its own article as needing better medical references [1].

A randomized trial published in 2006 in Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery compared post-treatment regimens with and without a copper tripeptide complex on CO2 laser-resurfaced skin and assessed erythema over the recovery period [11].

Wikipedia summarises rabbit wound studies from 2006 and 2008 reporting better contraction, faster granulation tissue and more blood vessel growth, and a 2003 rat study of ischemic skin flaps in which wound size fell by 64.5 percent with GHK, 45.6 percent with vehicle and 28.2 percent with no treatment [1]. A 1993 rat-wound study reported stimulated connective tissue accumulation, and other animal studies describe effects in lung injury models [36][37].

GHK is hydrophilic and charged at physiological pH, and the 2025 review reports that GHK-Cu permeation through intact skin is low in several experiments, for example 0.006 percent of the dose reaching the receptor phase through epidermis in one study versus 20 percent through isolated stratum corneum, and that no peptide or copper crossed intact human skin with microneedle pretreatment in another [27]. This has motivated liposomal and niosomal carriers, and the review concludes that permeability could be increased with enhancement methods [9][27]. Copper ligand exchange complicates measurement, since the peptide and the copper must be quantified separately [27].

Topical cosmetic products carry general warnings such as external use only and avoiding eyes [8]. The FDA states that compounded injectable GHK-Cu may pose a risk of immunogenicity because of aggregation and peptide-related impurities, and that human data to inform safety are limited [7]. Sports medicine reviewers describe gray-market peptides as operating outside regulatory oversight, with variable product quality [6].

Wikipedia notes that because GHK-Cu stimulates breakdown as well as synthesis of matrix components, its use should be approached with caution [1]. A T Nation poster who used a blend containing GHK-Cu suggested it might be pulling copper into the skin and linked it to low copper or iron absorption, citing online reports from others; no study tests that claim [15].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, GHK-Cu appears mostly as one component of multi-peptide blends. Users describe a product they call KLOW (KPV, BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu) taken daily for joints and soft tissue, with GHK-Cu described as the skin and hair component; others ask about a similar GLOW stack for post-surgery recovery, or list GHK-Cu among compounds in their cycles for skin and looks [17][18][19][20][21]. One poster says they inject a peptide mix including GHK-Cu into a bursa [22].

On looksmax.org, threads range from a 19-year-old with fine lines and atopic dermatitis asking whether the peptide's anti-inflammatory properties would help, to questions on whether it is better than Matrixyl for skin, how it compares with isotretinoin, and whether it is useful for acne; one thread title calls it 'cope for acne' [29][30][31][38][28]. Contributors often treat it as a skin-quality add-on within a broader appearance routine rather than a standalone fix.

Injectable GHK-Cu appears on FDA's list of bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks when used in compounding [7]. Sports medicine reviews published in 2026 describe a rapidly expanding use of approved and unapproved peptides outside regulatory oversight, and an Aesthetic Surgery Journal commentary titled 'Mechanistic plausibility should not be conflated with clinical validation of GHK-Cu' addresses the gap between laboratory findings and clinical proof [5][6][39].

Published human work on GHK-Cu is small. It includes a randomized trial of copper tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing [11] and the short controlled facial, eye and thigh studies summarized in reviews [1][2][12]. Registered studies include a phase 2 topical gel trial in acute wounds, a planned study of a patch and circulating GHK and GHK-Cu levels in 100 healthy adults, an early-phase study of systemic and topical interventions using aging clocks, and a Hydrafacial skin-quality trial [10][23][24][25]. Studies of injectable peptide therapy in sports medicine are primarily reviews of preclinical and limited human evidence [5][6][14].

timeline.event: Pilgeram and Pickart's fibrinogen work sets up the observation that older liver cells behave more like young cells in young blood [12][1].
Loren Pickart isolates GHK-Cu activity from human plasma albumin; reported in Nature in May [1].
The growth-modulating peptide is shown to be glycyl-histidyl-lysine [1].
Pickart and colleagues propose GHK helps move copper into cells [12].
Accelerated wound healing with GHK-Cu reported [12].
Stimulated collagen synthesis in fibroblast cultures reported [32].
Thigh-cream study reports higher procollagen synthesis with GHK-Cu than with vitamin C or retinoic acid creams [27].
GHK-Cu shown to stimulate matrix metalloproteinase-2 expression in fibroblasts [34].
Leyden and colleagues present 12-week facial and eye-cream studies [12].
Randomized trial of copper tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing is published [11].
Pickart and Margolina publish a gene-expression review of GHK-Cu [4].
Phase 2 trial of topical GHK-Cu gel for acute skin wounds begins recruiting [10].

lore.intro: GHK-Cu is discussed on T Nation chiefly as part of injectable peptide blends and as a skin and hair add-on to cycles, and on looksmax.org as a skin-quality peptide used topically, with microneedling, or by injection [17][21][28][29].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu in a peptide blend supports skin and hair as well as injury recovery
claims.believers: A poster says the GHK-Cu in a KLOW blend is the skin and hair component, while the other peptides address soft tissue and inflammation, and another describes using it daily for years of injuries [17][19].
claims.experts: Reviews describe collagen and gene-expression effects mainly from cell and animal work, with human cosmetic studies small; sports medicine reviews call evidence for injectable peptides limited [1][5][14].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu is a 'looksmax' peptide that improves skin and appearance
claims.believers: A poster planning a cycle lists GHK-Cu among peptides for skin and tan and 'to look better' [21].
claims.experts: Controlled studies of topical GHK-Cu are small and short [1]; no published trial tests injectable GHK-Cu for appearance.

claims.claim: GHK-Cu plus microneedling gives better skin results than the topical alone
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply states that topical GHK-Cu with microneedling is more effective than the topical on its own [28].
claims.experts: Reviews report low skin permeation of GHK-Cu through intact skin, and one cited experiment found no peptide or copper crossing intact human skin with microneedle pretreatment; no published trial compares the combination for appearance [27].

claims.claim: Falling GHK levels with age explain skin aging, so restoring GHK reverses it
claims.believers: Proponents cite the decline from about 200 ng/ml at age 20 to about 80 ng/ml by 60 as the reason to supplement [1][3].
claims.experts: The levels are reported in reviews, but the 2025 BioImpacts review calls clinical data scarce, and a 2026 commentary distinguishes mechanistic plausibility from clinical validation [1][27][39].

claims.claim: A topical GHK-Cu cream firms skin and smooths wrinkles
claims.believers: Company-affiliated authors describe 12-week studies in 41 to 71 women showing thicker, denser, firmer skin and fewer fine lines [12].
claims.experts: The 2025 review notes the human studies are small or available only as abstracts, and Wikipedia calls them small and short [1][27].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu 'resets' gene expression toward a younger state
claims.believers: The review authors report that GHK modulates about a third of human genes and increases DNA-repair gene expression [4][12].
claims.experts: The same authors state the gene analyses are computational and links to outcomes are inferred, not experimentally tested [4].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu can deplete copper or cause problems when taken in blends
claims.believers: One poster suspects a GHK-Cu blend was pulling copper into the skin and causing low iron-related problems, citing online reports [15].
claims.experts: No study tests this; the FDA instead cites immunogenicity risks for compounded injectables [7].

claims.claim: Injectable GHK-Cu is safe because it is a natural human peptide
claims.believers: Posters describe it as a naturally occurring peptide and use it routinely in stacks [17][19].
claims.experts: The FDA says compounded injectable GHK-Cu may pose a risk of immunogenicity through aggregation and impurities, with limited human data [7]; reviewers note gray-market quality variability [6].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu gives scar reduction and anti-aging
claims.believers: An older T Nation post links to a scar-reduction site promoting copper peptides for scar removal [26].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports animal wound-healing data and small human facial studies, with definitive conclusions awaiting more research [1].
